title: HTTP and HTTPS: a request, a code, a page
intro: Typing a web address starts a short conversation. Let's watch it, then see what the S in HTTPS protects.

predict.question: A snoop on cafe wifi watches your HTTPS login. What can they read?
options: Only scrambled bytes, not the content
Nothing, not even which server you talk to
predict.reveal: HTTPS encrypts the content, so the snoop only sees scrambled bytes. They can still tell which server you connected to.

takeaway: HTTP is request, status code, response. HTTPS wraps it in TLS so others on the network cannot read or alter it.

steps.say: You open https://shop.com. The browser must talk to the web server. A snoop shares the same cafe wifi. First, the secure connection.
After TCP connects, the browser starts the TLS handshake with ClientHello: the encryption methods it supports.
The server replies with its certificate, a signed ID card for shop.com, and picks the encryption method.
The browser checks the certificate is genuine and both sides agree on a secret key. Handshake done: everything now is encrypted.
Now the HTTP request: a method (GET), a path, and headers. Only the server can read it.
The server answers with a status code first. 200 OK means success, then the page itself follows.
A missing page gets a different code. 404 Not Found means the client asked for something that does not exist. 500 means the server broke.
Now imagine plain HTTP with no TLS. Everything travels as readable text, so the snoop can read the password.
With HTTPS the snoop gets only scrambled bytes. They can neither read nor quietly change the page on the way.
HTTPS gives privacy, integrity and proof you reached the real shop.com. Always look for the padlock before typing a password.
